posts.topic: Charge of the Light Brigade and Fenton's 'Valley of the Shadow of Death' photo
image_search: Valley of the shadow of death Fenton
Roger Fenton Valley of the Shadow of Death
posts.caption:
💣 ON THIS DAY in 1854, about 670 British cavalrymen charged into the "valley of Death". The famous photo tied to it hides a secret.

On 25 October 1854, at the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War, a vague, misunderstood order sent the Light Brigade straight at Russian guns. More than 100 men were killed. A French marshal who watched said: "It is magnificent, but it is not war."

Tennyson's poem made that valley immortal. So, in many minds, did a photograph: Roger Fenton's "The Valley of the Shadow of Death", a road littered with cannonballs.

But Fenton took it in 1855, near Sevastopol, several miles from where the Light Brigade charged.

And he made two exposures from the same spot. In one, the cannonballs lie in the ditch. In the other, they are scattered across the road.

Filmmaker Errol Morris and optical engineer Dennis Purcell compared small rocks on the slope, which had shifted downhill. Their conclusion: the famous version, cannonballs on the road, was taken second.

Is a staged war photo still an honest record of war?

posts.title: Einstein never failed math

scenes.narration: Einstein failing maths is one of history's favourite myths.
scenes.label: MYTH

scenes.narration: By his own account, he had mastered calculus before he turned fifteen.
scenes.label: AGE 15

scenes.narration: At sixteen, he took the entrance exam for the Zurich Polytechnic. He did best in maths and science.
His language and history results let him down, so he was told to finish school first.
scenes.label: REJECTED

scenes.narration: His 1896 school certificate in Aarau shows a 6, the top Swiss grade, in algebra, geometry and physics.
scenes.label: 6 OUT OF 6

scenes.narration: Later, Ripley's Believe It or Not ran the line: 'Greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics.'
scenes.label: RIPLEY'S
image_search: Robert Ripley Believe It or Not

scenes.narration: In 1935, a rabbi showed Einstein the clipping. He laughed and said: 'I never failed in mathematics.'
What school myth did you grow up believing? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🧮 MYTH vs FACT: Einstein never failed maths.

At 16 he fell short on a university entrance exam because of languages and history, while doing best in maths and science. His school certificate a year later shows top marks in algebra, geometry and physics.

Why do you think this myth is so popular?

posts.topic: Daguerre's Boulevard du Temple, the first photograph of a person (1838)
posts.caption:
📷 The first person ever photographed had no idea. He was just getting his boots shined.

In 1838, Louis Daguerre photographed the Boulevard du Temple, one of the busiest streets in Paris, from his studio.

The exposure took several minutes. Carriages, horses and crowds moved too fast to register, so the street looks almost deserted.

But in the lower left corner, one man stood still long enough to appear: a customer with his foot up, having his boots polished. It is the earliest known photograph of a human being.

The original plate survived an 1839 fire at Daguerre's studio. Later restoration attempts ruined it, and today we know the image mainly from photographs of the plate taken in the 1930s.

He never knew he had made history. Who do you think he was?

posts.topic: The Obelisk of Axum's return from Rome
posts.caption:
🏛️ LOST & FOUND: A 1,700-year-old stone giant was taken from Africa to Rome. It took 68 years to bring it home.

The Obelisk of Axum was carved in the 4th century AD in the ancient kingdom of Aksum, in today's northern Ethiopia. It stands about 24 metres tall, weighs more than 150 tonnes, and has false doors and windows carved into the stone.

In 1937, during Mussolini's occupation of Ethiopia, it was cut into three pieces and shipped to Rome, where it was raised at Piazza di Porta Capena.

In 1947, Italy agreed to return it. For decades, it stayed put. Then lightning struck it in Rome in the early 2000s.

In April 2005, the three pieces were flown back to Ethiopia aboard giant Antonov cargo planes. UNESCO teams reassembled it, and in September 2008 it stood again in Axum.

Would you travel to Ethiopia to see it back where it was made?

posts.topic: Flight 19, the lost Avenger squadron of 1945
posts.title: Five Planes Vanished: The Real Story of Flight 19 and the Bermuda Triangle

scenes.narration: At 6:20 on the evening of December 5, 1945, radio operators in Florida heard the last words from a flight of five Navy bombers lost over the Atlantic.
scenes.label: 5 DEC 1945
image_search: TBM Avengers of VT-88 in flight

scenes.narration: Fourteen men were aboard. None of them, and none of the planes, has ever been found. That night, a rescue plane with thirteen men vanished too.
scenes.label: 14 + 13 MEN

scenes.narration: Coming up: what the pilots said on the radio, what the Navy concluded, and how this one flight gave birth to the Bermuda Triangle legend.
Flight 19 was a training mission from Naval Air Station Fort Lauderdale. Five TBM Avenger torpedo bombers took off at 2:10 in the afternoon.
scenes.label: 2:10 PM

scenes.narration: The exercise was called Navigation Problem Number One: practice bombing at Hens and Chickens Shoals, then a three-leg route over the Bahamas and back to Florida.
scenes.label: NAV PROBLEM 1

scenes.narration: Most of the pilots were trainees. Their leader, Lieutenant Charles Taylor, was an instructor with about 2,500 flying hours and a combat tour in the Pacific.
scenes.label: LT. TAYLOR
image_search: Grumman TBM-3E Avenger of VT-81 in flight

scenes.narration: The Avenger was a big, rugged warplane built to carry a torpedo. The planes in Flight 19 each carried a crew of two or three.
image_search: Grumman TBM Avenger aboard USS Randolph

scenes.narration: The weather looked normal, with a few scattered showers. The practice bombing went as planned. Then, less than two hours after takeoff, things began to go wrong.
Radio operators overheard a pilot say: 'I don't know where we are. We must have got lost after that last turn.'
scenes.label: ~4:00 PM

scenes.narration: Taylor radioed that both his compasses were out. The Navy later concluded that he believed the islands below him were the Florida Keys.
If that were true, flying east would bring them home. But radio bearings placed the planes north of the Bahamas, far out over the Atlantic.
scenes.label: WRONG WAY?

scenes.narration: One airman was heard saying: 'If we could just fly west, we would get home.' The flight changed course again and again as daylight faded.
image_search: TBM Avengers of VT-88 in flight

scenes.narration: Ground stations asked Taylor to switch to the emergency rescue frequency. He refused, saying he had to keep his planes together.
The weather worsened and night fell over a rough sea. The final message said that when the first plane dropped below ten gallons, they would all go down together.
scenes.label: 6:20 PM
image_search: TBM Avengers of VT-88 in flight in August 1945

scenes.narration: Rescue aircraft went out. At 7:27 p.m., a PBM Mariner flying boat took off from Naval Air Station Banana River with thirteen men aboard.
scenes.label: 7:27 PM
image_search: Martin PBM-5 Mariner in flight c1945

scenes.narration: It made a routine radio call a few minutes later. Then it disappeared from radar and was never heard from again.
At 9:15 p.m., the tanker Gaines Mills reported a burst of flame about 100 feet high on the sea, and an oil slick. No survivors were found.
scenes.label: 9:15 PM

scenes.narration: Mariners were known to be prone to such accidents. The Navy concluded the flying boat most likely exploded in mid-air, soon after takeoff.
image_search: Martin PBM-3 Mariner in flight c1942

scenes.narration: For about five days, ships and aircraft searched some 300,000 square miles of ocean. They found no trace of Flight 19.
scenes.label: 300,000 SQ MI

scenes.narration: A Navy board concluded that Taylor had mistaken his position and led the flight out to sea, where the planes ran out of fuel and came down.
Taylor's mother objected that her son was being blamed with no planes and no bodies as evidence. The Navy changed its finding to 'cause unknown'.
scenes.label: CAUSE UNKNOWN

scenes.narration: That open verdict fed a mystery. In 1964, writer Vincent Gaddis linked Flight 19 to other losses in an Argosy magazine article, 'The Deadly Bermuda Triangle'.
Later researchers found many Bermuda Triangle stories exaggerated or impossible to verify. For Flight 19, the likeliest explanation is simpler: lost, out of fuel, ditching in a dark sea.
Avenger wrecks have been found off Florida, but none has been proven to be from Flight 19. Five Avengers found on the seabed in 1991 turned out to be different planes.
Fourteen men and five planes are still out there somewhere. Do you accept the Navy's first explanation, or do you think there is more to this story?
image_search: TBM Avengers of VT-88 in flight

posts.caption:
✈️ UNSOLVED FILES: On 5 December 1945, five US Navy Avenger bombers left Fort Lauderdale on a training flight. They never came back. That night, a rescue plane with 13 men vanished too.

The radio calls, the Navy's verdict, and how one lost flight created the Bermuda Triangle legend.

Do you accept the Navy's first explanation?

posts.topic: Violet Jessop, survivor of the Olympic, Titanic and Britannic
posts.title: The woman who survived three sister-ship disasters
posts.hook_text: SHE SURVIVED ALL THREE SISTER SHIPS

scenes.narration: One woman was aboard all three sister ships when disaster struck.
scenes.label: 3 SHIPS

scenes.narration: Violet Jessop, born in Argentina to Irish parents, went to sea as a stewardess.
September 1911: her ship, the Olympic, collided with the cruiser HMS Hawke. Both stayed afloat.
April 1912: she was a stewardess on the Titanic. She escaped in a lifeboat as it sank.
An officer handed her a baby to hold. On the rescue ship, a woman took it back without a word of thanks.
scenes.label: TITANIC

scenes.narration: November 1916: now a wartime nurse, she was aboard the hospital ship Britannic when it hit a mine.
Her lifeboat was pulled toward the spinning propellers. She jumped, though she couldn't swim, and fractured her skull. She survived.
scenes.label: KEA, 1916

scenes.narration: Lucky, or cursed? What do you think? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🚢 Violet Jessop was aboard the Olympic when it collided with HMS Hawke in 1911, the Titanic when it sank in 1912, and the hospital ship Britannic when it sank in 1916.

She survived all three, and lived to 84.

Would you have gone back to sea after the Titanic?
